1.title: hello, goodbye, peace
1.hook: hello, goodbye, peace — and a fourth meaning: whole
1.howItsDone: Many Jews say shalom as hello and goodbye, and Shabbat shalom on the Sabbath; the priestly blessing, which ends with a prayer for peace, is said in synagogue and by many parents over their children on Friday night.

segments.voice: Walk into a café in Tel Aviv and listen to one word do three jobs. Someone comes in: shalom. Someone leaves: shalom. And on a greeting card, at the end of a letter, over a door: shalom, peace. Hello, goodbye, peace. It's one of the few words anywhere that works at both ends of a conversation. You may have heard it in a movie, or from a friend, or at a wedding. But there's a fourth meaning hiding underneath the other three, and it's the one the rest of them grow from. Today, the first word on this path, and the wish that's folded inside it.

Shalom is Hebrew. Like most Hebrew words it grows from a root of three letters, shin, lamed, mem, and the root's first sense isn't quiet. It's whole. Complete. Nothing missing. The same root gives Hebrew shalem, whole, and a verb for paying back what you owe, so the account is square again. So peace, in this language, isn't only the absence of a fight. It's the presence of everything that should be there. A house with shalom has nothing broken in it. A body with shalom is well. When the Bible asks how someone is, it asks after their shalom. In Genesis, Jacob sends his son Joseph to check on his brothers, and the Hebrew says, more or less: go and see the shalom of your brothers. How whole are they? The word runs all through Jewish prayer. The priestly blessing, still said over congregations, and by many parents over their children on Friday night, ends with it. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace." Peace is the last word. Many central Jewish prayers close by asking for it too. And the Psalms don't treat peace as something that just happens to you. They say: "seek peace, and pursue it." The rabbis noticed that verb. Most good deeds, they taught, you do when the chance comes to you. Peace you go after. You chase it. So when someone says shalom at a door, coming or going, underneath the hello is an old wish: may you be whole. May nothing be missing.
screen: `SH-L-M — WHOLE, COMPLETE.` · `SEE THE SHALOM OF YOUR BROTHERS.` · `THE BLESSING ENDS IN PEACE.` · `SEEK PEACE, AND PURSUE IT.` · then, large: `MAY NOTHING BE MISSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for day one, and it's small on purpose. One breath, with the bell. Breathe in slowly, and notice one place in you that feels not quite whole right now. Tired. Worried. Rushed. On the way out, if you want to, say the word, out loud or inside: shalom. Not to fix anything. Just to wish it whole.
Shalom. Hello, goodbye, peace, and underneath all three: whole, with nothing missing. First word on your strand.

segments.voice: Your line to carry: be whole. Once today, when you say hello or goodbye to someone, mean the old wish inside it: may nothing be missing for you. That's day one. You showed up. See you tomorrow.

2.title: six words
2.hook: six words; the sentence a Jew says with eyes covered
2.howItsDone: Jews traditionally say the Shema in the morning and evening prayers and again at bedtime, covering the eyes with the right hand for the first line; many parents say it with their children as they fall asleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shalom. Hello, goodbye, peace, and underneath all three, whole. Did you catch yourself wishing someone whole? Day two.

Picture a synagogue on an ordinary morning. People are reading, murmuring, some standing, some swaying. Then, at one moment, many of them do the same small thing. They raise a hand and cover their eyes. For a few seconds a room full of adults sits like children playing hide and seek. And under the hands, six Hebrew words. It's the first prayer many Jewish children learn, often at bedtime, and by long tradition it's meant to be among the last words a person says in this life. Six words, said at the beginning and the end. Today: the sentence under the hand.
screen: `A HAND OVER THE EYES.` → `SIX HEBREW WORDS.` → `THE FIRST PRAYER AND THE LAST.`

segments.voice: The six words are: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one." It comes from the book of Deuteronomy, and it's named for its first word. Shema. Hear. But the Hebrew verb is bigger than hearing with your ears. It means listen, pay attention, understand, and even take it to heart and act on it. It's not "here is a fact." It's "are you listening?" Notice who it's said to. Not to God. To Israel, to the people, to the person saying it. It's a sentence you say to yourself, out loud, to wake yourself up. A detail about the name. The word written there is God's four-letter name, which Jewish tradition doesn't pronounce. Reading aloud, people say Adonai, my Lord, instead. And a detail about the page. In a handwritten Torah scroll, two letters in this verse are written extra large: the last letter of the first word and the last letter of the last word. Together they spell ed, the Hebrew word for witness. Saying it, many teachers say, is a kind of testimony. Why the hand over the eyes? The Talmud remembers that Rabbi Judah the Prince, who compiled the Mishnah, passed his hand over his eyes when he said it. People still do. Shut out everything you can see, just for a moment, so you can hear. The same passage says to speak these words when you lie down and when you rise up. So it's said morning and night, and at bedtime, and at the end.
screen: `SHEMA — HEAR, LISTEN, TAKE IT IN.` · `SAID TO ISRAEL, NOT TO GOD.` · `TWO BIG LETTERS SPELL WITNESS.` · `A HAND OVER THE EYES, TO HEAR.` · then, large: `HEAR, O ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: One breath, with the bell. Cover your eyes with one hand, the way people do for the Shema. Let the room disappear. Breathe in slowly and just listen, to whatever sound is left: a fan, traffic, your own breath. If you pray, you can say the six words on the way out. If not, let the breath out and simply hear.
The Shema. Six words that begin hear, O Israel, said morning and night with the eyes covered. Second word.
Your line: hear. Once today, when someone is talking to you, stop doing the other thing, look up, and actually listen to the end of their sentence. Day two.

3.title: the oldest labor law
3.hook: the oldest labor law; a day the world can't have
3.tomorrow: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset
3.howItsDone: Jews mark Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall with candles, blessings over wine and bread, a family meal and synagogue; observant Jews refrain from the thirty-nine categories of work, while many others keep it through the meal, rest and a slower day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Shema. Six words, eyes covered, that begin with hear. Did you listen to someone all the way to the end of a sentence? Day three.

Think about your phone on a Saturday. Work email. The group chat. A sale that ends tonight. The world never really closes anymore. Now picture a whole family, every week, for twenty-five hours, where none of that gets in. No office. No shopping. Many don't even switch on a light. Not because it's a holiday, and not because someone is sick. Just because it's the seventh day. People have been doing this for something like three thousand years, through empires, exile and poverty, and it may be the oldest rule anywhere that says a worker gets a day off. Today: the day the world can't have.
screen: `THE WORLD NEVER CLOSES.` → `TWENTY-FIVE HOURS IT CAN'T REACH.` → `THE SEVENTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root, shin, bet, tav, that means to stop. To cease. Not first to relax, or to worship, but to stop. English borrowed it as Sabbath. It runs from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday, when three stars are out, because in the Torah's story a day starts in the evening. Now the labor law. When the Torah gives the Sabbath rule in Deuteronomy, it doesn't only say you rest. It lists who rests with you: your children, your servants, your animals, the stranger living in your town. And it gives the reason: "And thou shalt remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt." You know what it's like to work without end. So nobody in your house does. A weekly day off, for everyone, written down in the ancient world. The rabbis then asked a practical question: what counts as work? They found their answer in the Torah's description of building the tabernacle, the tent for God in the desert, and counted thirty-nine kinds of creative work: planting, baking, writing, building, lighting a fire, and more. On Shabbat, those stop. Jews keep this in different ways. Orthodox Jews keep the thirty-nine categories carefully, so no driving, no cooking, no phones. Many Conservative, Reform and other Jews keep Shabbat through the candles, the meal, synagogue, and a slower day, each deciding how much to set down. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described Shabbat as a kind of palace built in time rather than space. You don't travel to it. It arrives, every week, wherever you are.
screen: `SHABBAT — TO STOP.` · `YOU WERE A SERVANT IN EGYPT.` · `THIRTY-NINE KINDS OF WORK.` · `A PALACE IN TIME.` · then, large: `FRIDAY SUNSET TO SATURDAY STARS.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. On each breath, put one thing down. First breath: set down the thing you're working on. Second breath: set down the thing you're worried about. Third breath: set down the phone, if it's in your hand. For three breaths, nothing is being made or fixed. That's the whole idea of Shabbat, very small.
Shabbat. To stop. The seventh day, sunset Friday to stars on Saturday, a rest for everyone in the house. Third word.
Your line: stop. it's already Friday. Whatever day it actually is, pick one small stretch today, ten minutes, and treat it like the week is over. Nothing to finish. Day three.

4.title: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset
4.hook: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset — why sunset is the clock
4.howItsDone: In many Jewish homes a woman of the house, or anyone present, lights at least two candles before sunset on Friday, circles her hands over them, covers her eyes and says the blessing, and Shabbat begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabbat. To stop, from Friday sunset to Saturday stars. Your line was stop. it's already Friday. Did you find ten minutes with nothing to finish? Day four.

It's Friday afternoon in a Jewish home, and the clock is running. The oven is on. Someone is still in the shower. A kid can't find their shoes. Then, at a set minute, printed on a calendar on the fridge, it all has to be done. Someone stands at the table, strikes a match, and lights two candles. They circle their hands over the flames three times, cover their eyes, and whisper a blessing. When they uncover their eyes, the week is over. Eighteen minutes before sunset, in many towns. Today: two small flames, and why the sun keeps the clock.
screen: `FRIDAY. THE CLOCK IS RUNNING.` → `A MATCH, TWO FLAMES.` → `HANDS OVER THE EYES.`

segments.voice: Start with the clock. In the first chapter of the Torah, every day of creation closes the same way. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Evening first. So a Jewish day begins at sunset, and Shabbat arrives with the dark on Friday. The candles are lit before sunset, because lighting a fire is one of the kinds of work that stop on Shabbat. Many communities light eighteen minutes early, a margin, so nobody is caught lighting late. Jerusalem traditionally lights forty minutes before. Why two? Because the Sabbath commandment appears twice in the Torah, in two wordings. In Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." In Deuteronomy: "Observe the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Remember and observe. Zachor and shamor. One flame for each. Many families add a candle for every child, so the table gets brighter as the family grows. Then the eyes. Usually you say a blessing and then do the thing. But once the blessing is said, Shabbat has begun and lighting is no longer allowed. So people light first, cover their eyes, say the blessing, and then open them, as if seeing the light for the first time. And why candles at all? The Talmud asks: if you're poor, and can only afford one light, and it's both Shabbat and Hanukkah, which do you buy? The Shabbat light, it says, for the sake of peace in the home. Shalom bayit. Not a light to read by. A light so the family can see each other's faces at dinner.
screen: `EVENING FIRST, THEN MORNING.` · `REMEMBER, AND OBSERVE.` · `LIGHT, THEN BLESS, THEN SEE.` · `A LIGHT FOR PEACE IN THE HOME.` · then, large: `TWO FLAMES.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. If there's a light near you, a lamp or a candle or even your screen, look at it. First breath: remember something good from this week. Second breath: let it be enough. Third breath: close your eyes, the way people do after lighting, and then open them slowly, as if the light is new.
The candles. Two flames lit before sunset on Friday, remember and observe, for peace in the home. Fourth word.
Your line: light, then rest. Tonight, before you stop for the day, turn on one light on purpose, a lamp or a candle, and let it mean the work is done. Day four.

5.title: the blessing before eating
5.hook: the blessing before eating; saying thank you to the source
5.howItsDone: Observant Jews say a short blessing before eating or drinking, with a different ending for bread, fruit, vegetables, wine and other foods, and a longer grace after meals, the Birkat Hamazon, after eating bread.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the candles. Two flames before sunset, remember and observe. Your line was light, then rest. Did one light tell you the day was done? Day five.

Watch someone who keeps this tradition pick up an apple. Before the first bite there's a pause, about two seconds long, and a murmur you'd miss if you weren't looking. Then the bite. Same with a glass of water. A cookie. A piece of bread at a wedding. Most of us eat the way we scroll: mid-sentence, standing up, already thinking about the next thing. This is the opposite. A tiny speed bump between wanting something and having it. And the words inside that pause have a surprising reason behind them. Today: the two-second blessing.
screen: `AN APPLE. A PAUSE.` → `TWO SECONDS, A MURMUR.` → `THEN THE BITE.`

segments.voice: A bracha is a blessing. Almost every one begins the same way: baruch atah Adonai, eloheinu melech ha-olam, roughly, blessed are you, Lord our God, ruler of the world. Then the ending changes with the food. For bread: who brings forth bread from the earth. For fruit: who creates the fruit of the tree. For water, or almost anything else: by whose word all things came to be. Here's the surprise. It's not the food being blessed. The blessing is said to the source of the food. Why bother? The Talmud notices two verses that seem to disagree. One psalm says: "The earth is the LORD'S, and the fulness thereof." Another says: "The heavens are the heavens of the LORD; but the earth hath He given to the children of men." Which is it? Does the world belong to God, or to us? The rabbis' answer: both, and the blessing is the hinge. Before the blessing, the apple is still God's. After it, it's been given to you. To eat without a blessing, the Talmud says, is a little like taking something that isn't yours yet. There's a blessing after eating too. Deuteronomy says: "And thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God." First eat, then be full, then say thanks, which is the order most of us would actually manage. One rabbi of the Talmud, Rabbi Meir, taught that a person should say a hundred blessings every day. It sounds like a lot until you notice how many things you do in a day without noticing any of them. A hundred small pauses.
screen: `BLESSED ARE YOU, THE SOURCE.` · `THE EARTH IS THE LORD'S.` · `BUT THE EARTH HE HATH GIVEN.` · `A HUNDRED BLESSINGS A DAY.` · then, large: `THE BLESSING IS THE HINGE.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. If there's something to eat or drink near you, hold it, even a glass of water. First breath: look at it. Second breath: think of one hand it passed through to reach you, a farmer, a driver, a cashier. Third breath: if you pray, you can say a blessing you know. If not, just say thank you, to wherever it came from. Then drink.
Bracha. A blessing, said to the source before you eat, and after you're full. Fifth word.
Your line: notice before you bite. At every meal today, even a snack in the car, give it two seconds first. Look at it. Then eat. Day five.

6.title: "and it was good"
6.howItsDone: Jews read Genesis 1 in synagogue at the start of the yearly Torah cycle, in the autumn, and the verses about the seventh day that follow it open the Friday-night kiddush in many homes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bracha. A blessing said to the source, before you eat. Your line was notice before you bite. Did a snack get its two seconds? Day six.

You know the feeling. You finish something, a painted wall, a clean kitchen, a hard email, and before you move on, you stand back and look at it. Just for a second. Not to fix anything. Just to see it. The very first chapter of the Torah is built around that moment. Something is made, and then the maker stands back and looks. And the same short line comes back again and again, like the chorus of a song. Count it, and you get seven. Today: the first chapter, and the line that keeps coming back.
screen: `YOU FINISH SOMETHING.` → `YOU STAND BACK AND LOOK.` → `THE SAME LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Genesis one is the story of six days of making. Light. Sky. Land and plants. Sun, moon and stars. Fish and birds. Animals, and then people. We'll walk through the days slowly when the stories begin. Today, just the refrain. In the Hebrew, two words: ki tov. That it was good. The first time is right after the light. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And God saw the light, that it was good." God doesn't only make. God looks. Count the refrain through the chapter and it comes seven times, and seven is the number this chapter is built on. Now the details the rabbis loved. On the second day, when the sky separates the waters, the line is missing. No good. One old explanation: the work of the waters wasn't finished until the next day, and you don't call something good halfway through. Then the third day gets it twice. That's why some Jews still like to hold weddings on Tuesday, the third day of the Jewish week: a day of double good. And the seventh time is different. At the very end, God looks at everything together, the people, the animals, the stars, all of it: "And God saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was very good." Not each piece alone. The whole. Good, in Hebrew, isn't a grade for perfect. The chapter doesn't say flawless. It says good. It works. It belongs. And the first reaction to the world in the Torah isn't a rule or a warning. It's somebody looking at it, and liking what they see.
screen: `KI TOV — THAT IT WAS GOOD.` · `THE SECOND DAY: NO GOOD YET.` · `THE THIRD DAY: GOOD, TWICE.` · `ALL OF IT TOGETHER: VERY GOOD.` · then, large: `AND GOD SAW THAT IT WAS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Look around wherever you are. On the first breath, find one thing that's made well, a cup, a chair, a tree outside. On the second, find one living thing, even just your own hand. On the third, take in the whole room at once, and let the word land on it, out loud or inside: good.
Genesis one. The first chapter of the Torah, where God makes and then looks, seven times: good, and at the end, very good. Sixth word.
Your line: it was good. Today, when you finish anything, even washing a mug, stop for one second and look at it before you move on. Day six.

7.title: even the animals rest
7.tomorrow: the man who argued with God about Sodom
7.howItsDone: Jews read both versions of the Ten Commandments in the yearly Torah cycle, and many sing a Friday-night hymn, Lecha Dodi, whose opening line speaks of remember and observe being said as one word.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Genesis 1, and the refrain that comes seven times. Your line was it was good. Did you stop and look at one finished thing? Day seven, the end of your first week.

Picture a farm three thousand years ago, on the seventh day. The family isn't working. Fine. But look closer. The hired hand isn't working either. The foreign worker who lives at the edge of the village is sitting in the shade. And the ox, the one that pulls the plow six days a week, is standing in the field doing absolutely nothing, and nobody is allowed to put it to work. In an age when almost nobody thought twice about a donkey's day off, one law wrote the animals in. Today, at the end of week one: the commandment that rests everyone.
screen: `A FARM ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` → `THE WORKER RESTS.` → `EVEN THE OX RESTS.`

segments.voice: The Sabbath commandment is one of the Ten Words given at Sinai, the fourth in the Jewish count, and it's the longest of them. It appears twice in the Torah, in two slightly different versions, and the difference is the lesson. In Exodus it begins: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." And the reason given is creation: in six days God made the world, and on the seventh God rested. Rest is built into the world, the way we saw yesterday, when the six days of making come to an end. In Deuteronomy, Moses repeats it, and it begins: "Observe the sabbath day, to keep it holy." This time the reason is different. It's Egypt. You were slaves, so rest: "that thy man-servant and thy maid-servant may rest as well as thou." As well as you. Not after you. Not instead of you. The same. Both versions list who rests: you, your son, your daughter, the servants, the stranger in your town, and the animals. Another law in Exodus puts it more plainly still, rest on the seventh day, "that thine ox and thine ass may have rest." The rabbis read those two versions as one. Remember and observe, they said, were spoken in a single utterance, the way only God could say two things at once. That's the two candles from day four. And so rest here isn't a treat you earn once your work is done. It's owed to everyone, and especially to whoever works for you.
screen: `REMEMBER — BECAUSE OF CREATION.` · `OBSERVE — BECAUSE OF EGYPT.` · `AS WELL AS THOU.` · `THE OX AND THE ASS REST TOO.` · then, large: `REST IS OWED.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell, and a look back at your first week: shalom, the Shema, Shabbat, the candles, bracha, Genesis one, and today. On the first breath, think of someone who works so your life runs, a driver, a cleaner, a parent. On the second, wish them a real rest. On the third, give yourself one too.
The Sabbath commandment. Remember, and observe: rest, for you, your household, the stranger and even the animals. Seventh word. A full week.
Your line: rest is for everyone. Today, make someone else's load lighter by one thing: a thank you, a task you take off them, an early finish. Day seven. Week one, done.

twice: remember in Exodus, observe in Deuteronomy.
the commandment includes animals

options: because you were slaves in Egypt.
